title: Korean War
summary: A three-year war on the Korean Peninsula that began when North Korean forces crossed the 38th parallel on 25 June 1950, drew in a US-led United Nations command and China, killed millions of Koreans, and ended in an armistice, not a peace treaty.
card: North Korea attacked South Korea on 25 June 1950 with Soviet backing, and the UN Security Council authorised a US-led defence. After the Inchon landing, the Chinese intervention and a long stalemate, an armistice was signed at Panmunjom on 27 July 1953. Estimates of the dead run from well under two million to about five million, mostly Korean, and no peace treaty has ever been signed.
what:
The Korean War was fought on the Korean Peninsula from 25 June 1950 until an armistice took effect at 22:00 on 27 July 1953. It began when the Korean People's Army of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, in the north, crossed the 38th parallel into the Republic of Korea in the south. Korea had been divided at that line by the United States and the Soviet Union at the end of the Second World War, and each power then backed a rival government, led by Kim Il Sung in the north and Syngman Rhee in the south. Soviet records released in the 1990s show that Kim planned the attack and that Stalin gave a conditional go-ahead during Kim's secret visit to Moscow in April 1950.

The UN Security Council found a breach of the peace on 25 June, recommended on 27 June that members help South Korea, and on 7 July created a unified command under the United States. Northern forces took Seoul within days and by August had pushed UN and South Korean forces back to the Pusan Perimeter in the south-east. A US-led amphibious landing at Inchon on 15 September and the recapture of Seoul by 28 September reversed the war. UN forces then crossed the 38th parallel in October, and China entered the war on 19 October as the Chinese People's Volunteers, pushing the front back south. Seoul changed hands four times in all. After failed Chinese and North Korean offensives in April and May 1951 the front stabilised close to the old line, and talks that began in July 1951 dragged on for two more years while fighting and bombing continued.

The armistice of 27 July 1953 fixed a Military Demarcation Line with a four-kilometre demilitarised zone. It was signed by military commanders, not governments, and was never followed by a peace treaty. The human cost fell chiefly on Koreans: scholars estimate around 5 million deaths in all, including over 3 million civilians, with large uncertainty. Civilians died in bombing, in famine and flight, and in massacres committed by both sides and by US troops.

uncertainty.note: The dates 25 June 1950 and 27 July 1953 are those on which the open attack began and the armistice took effect, and are not in dispute. Border fighting along the 38th parallel was frequent between 1945 and 1950, so some historians treat the war as starting earlier (Yuh 2015, note 2). The armistice ended combat but not the legal state of war, so the war is also described as unended (Yuh 2015).

how: Three conditions made the war. First, the 1945 division at the 38th parallel set up two rival Korean states, each backed by a superpower and each claiming the whole peninsula. Second, Kim Il Sung sought Stalin's approval for a military reunification, and Soviet records show Stalin agreeing conditionally in April 1950, Mao Zedong approving in May, and Soviet advisers helping to plan the attack at divisional level while being withdrawn from the front before it began. Third, Stalin and Kim expected the United States not to intervene, since US forces had left the south. The Korean People's Army massed along the parallel from 12 to 23 June and attacked on 25 June. The sequence then followed the military balance: collapse of the south to the Pusan Perimeter, the Inchon landing that cut the northern supply line through Seoul, a UN advance towards the Yalu that alarmed Beijing, Chinese intervention that drove the front back, and a stalemate from mid-1951 as both sides dug in and negotiated.
why_it_matters: The war turned the 1945 occupation line into a permanent border between two hostile states. The armistice of 1953 never became a peace treaty, so the peninsula is still technically at war, about 130,000 people are registered with South Korea as members of separated families and the demilitarised zone still separates the armies. The war also reshaped the Cold War. The United States returned to the Asian mainland, fortified Japan as an ally through the 1951 treaties, and placed a UN-flagged command under American leadership; China's clash with the United States shaped its isolation and its alliance with Moscow for a generation. For Koreans the cost was extreme: perhaps one in ten died, more than half the dead were civilians, and the bombing of the north left it with little standing infrastructure, while massacres by both Korean governments and by US troops left grievances that truth commissions are still documenting. Without the invasion of June 1950, Korea might well have stayed a divided but less militarised peninsula, and the American security commitment in East Asia might have remained narrower; had Chinese forces not crossed the Yalu, UN forces might have occupied the whole north. Historians cannot be sure of such counterfactuals, but they show how much of the later East Asian order was set in these three years.

related.because: The Allied victory over Japan ended Japanese rule in Korea, and the United States and the Soviet Union agreed to split the peninsula at the 38th parallel, creating the two rival states that fought in 1950.
Stalin gave Kim Il Sung a conditional approval in April 1950, supplied arms and advisers, and thereby made the northern attack feasible.
The communist victory in China gave Kim a second patron whose approval he sought in Beijing in May 1950, and later supplied the army that intervened.

beats.caption: At the end of the Second World War the United States and the Soviet Union agree to split Korea at the 38th parallel. Each backs a rival government, and by 1950 neither Korean state accepts the line as a border.

beats.action: arrows.advance { from: 'north of 38th parallel', to: 'south', label: 'Korean People\'s Army attack', depth_km: '3-5 in first three hours' }
beats.caption: Before dawn on 25 June 1950 the Korean People's Army attacks along the parallel, after a Soviet-advised plan approved in outline by Stalin in April. Its units advance 3 to 5 kilometres in the first three hours.
The Security Council calls for a halt on 25 June, recommends help for South Korea on 27 June, and on 7 July creates a unified command under the United States. A UN force enters the war.

beats.action: front.hold { region: 'Pusan Perimeter', extent: 'about 75 miles north to south' }
beats.caption: By August the Korean People's Army has pushed UN and South Korean troops into a perimeter around Busan in the south-east. Most of the peninsula is under northern control.
On 15 September about 70,000 men land from 230 ships at Inchon. UN forces retake Seoul by 28 September, cut the northern supply line and force the northern army to retreat.

beats.caption: The UN approves crossing the 38th parallel on 7 October, and UN forces advance north. On 19 October Chinese People's Volunteers enter Korea. China's leaders had hoped to hold the north behind a line from Pyongyang to Wonsan.

beats.caption: Seoul changes hands four times. About 3 million civilians become refugees, and the United States drops 635,000 tons of bombs, including 32,557 tons of napalm, mostly on the north. Aggregate figures for the whole war.
In July 1950 US troops kill refugees at Nogeun-ri, with 250 to 300 dead by the memorial account. South Korean forces execute thousands of prisoners and Bodo League members at Busan, Masan and Jinju.
After failed offensives in April and May 1951, the Chinese and North Korean armies dig in. By August the war becomes a stalemate, and talks begin in July 1951.

perspectives.holder: United Nations Security Council, Republic of Korea and United States
perspectives.account: The war began with an unprovoked armed attack by North Korea across the 38th parallel on 25 June 1950; the Security Council found a breach of the peace and called on North Korean forces to withdraw to the parallel.

perspectives.holder: Democratic People's Republic of Korea, as told to its troops in June 1950
perspectives.account: Troops were told that the South Korean army had provoked a military attack across the 38th parallel and that the northern army was going over to a counterattack. Soviet reports of the time and later archival research show instead that the northern leadership planned the offensive in advance with Soviet help.

perspectives.holder: Chen Jian, Allen Whiting, Shen Zhihua and Donggil Kim (historians of China's entry)
perspectives.account: Whiting saw Chinese intervention as a reluctant response to the US advance towards the Yalu. Chen Jian stressed Mao's revolutionary aims. Shen Zhihua argues that Mao went ahead despite Stalin's refusal of prompt air cover to win Soviet guarantees and aid. Kim argues that Beijing expected UN forces to halt on a Pyongyang-Wonsan line if China sent troops, and that securing the northern part of North Korea was the chief aim.

perspectives.holder: US Army (2001 review) versus Associated Press journalists and Korean survivors
perspectives.account: The Army's No Gun Ri review of 1999-2001 concluded that the killings of refugees in July 1950 were not deliberate and that no orders to shoot were issued there. Charles Hanley, an Associated Press correspondent who helped confirm the massacre, argues that investigators set aside documents showing a policy of firing on approaching refugees. The Army later acknowledged seeing the Muccio letter but called it a proposed policy. Survivors' accounts and the memorial park state 250 to 300 dead.

Published totals disagree widely. Yuh, drawing on Cumings and a battle-deaths dataset, gives about 5 million dead; older compilations give Chinese military deaths of 110,000 to 1,000,000, and combined North Korean military and civilian deaths of 500,000 to 1,535,000. Differences arise from counting wounded, missing and non-combat deaths and from the absence of reliable northern and Chinese records.

numbers.label: Estimated soldiers and civilians killed in the Korean War
numbers.note: Single scholarly figure ('an estimated 5 million'); Yuh's note 1 says casualty statistics differ among sources depending on how deaths are counted. Older compilations give lower totals; see the military and combined ranges below.

numbers.label: Korean civilians killed
numbers.note: Yuh gives 'more than 3 million', about 10 percent of Korea's 30 million people in 1950, including victims of massacres and political executions by both sides. Other scholars give lower civilian totals; no source opened gives a lower figure directly.

numbers.label: South Korean civilian casualties, official count (killed, wounded, kidnapped and missing)
numbers.note: Official figure of the Institute for National Defense and Military Affairs (1996), including 764,281 men; it includes wounded, kidnapped and missing, so it is not a death toll.

numbers.label: South Korean military deaths
numbers.note: Yuh's figure from Lacina and Gleditsch's battle-deaths dataset, Halberstam and Cumings.

numbers.label: North Korean military deaths
numbers.note: Yuh's figure; compilations in src-kwe place North Korean military dead between 130,000 and 520,000, so the range of published estimates is wide.

numbers.label: Chinese military deaths
numbers.note: Range across published compilations (from 110,000 killed in action plus 35,000 other, to 1,000,000). Yuh gives about 600,000 and Weathersby says losses ran to many hundreds of thousands. China did not publish a detailed official count in sources opened.

numbers.label: South Korean military and civilian deaths combined, published compilations
numbers.note: Range across compilations: 415,004 killed (Leckie, Wallechinsky, Clodfelter, citing the US Defense Department) to 1,300,000 (Britannica).

numbers.label: North Korean military and civilian deaths combined, published compilations
United States military deaths
numbers.note: Most reliable count in the literature (US Department of Defense). Yuh rounds to 36,000; the Korean War Educator lists the official 33,741 battle deaths plus 2,827 other deaths.

numbers.label: Korean civilians who became refugees
numbers.note: Yuh, drawing on Cumings; she adds that about 1 million fled south before the war began.

numbers.label: Bombs dropped by the United States on Korea, including napalm
numbers.note: Includes 32,557 tons of napalm; figure from Armstrong and Cumings as cited by Yuh; dropped mostly on the north.

numbers.label: People registered as members of separated families with South Korea's Ministry of Unification
numbers.note: Yuh notes that estimates of all separated by the war run to about 2 million, and a 2005 survey found just over 700,000 South Koreans reporting direct relatives in the north.

numbers.label: Villagers killed at Nogeun-ri, late July 1950
numbers.note: Estimate attributed to the No Gun Ri Peace Park; the US Army has given no figure.

numbers.label: Prisoners and Bodo League members, killed by South Korean forces in 1950
numbers.note: Low end: more than 3,400 killed in the southern areas verified so far by the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, with 576 victims individually identified at the time. High end: about 200,000 of more than 300,000 league members allegedly killed in the war.

audience_note: This record describes mass death and atrocity, including aerial bombing of towns, massacres of unarmed civilians and prisoners by North Korean, South Korean, US and other forces, sexual exploitation of women, and the deaths of children. Photographs of refugees and of war damage may be distressing.

importance.justification: The war killed millions, made the Korean division permanent, drew in the United States, the Soviet Union and China, and defined Cold War Asia down to the present.
